pattern.description: Shell with a concave spire, white ground colour with golden blotches and dark brown tent-like markings; living animal white mottled with tan, siphon banded black and red.

egg.text: Across the genus, eggs are laid about once a year in capsules on the substrate; a figure of roughly 25,000 eggs per egg mass comes from two other cone species, not C. textile directly.

larva.text: The genus-wide pelagic veliger stage lasts about 1-50 days based on a study of a different species; C. textile larvae have been reared through this stage in captivity, but no confirmed duration specific to this species was found.

maturity.text: Age at sexual maturity is not established for C. textile in the sources reviewed.

lifespan.text: A genus-wide reference estimates cone snail lifespan at about 10 to 20 years based on shell growth marks; this is not confirmed specifically for C. textile.

deaths.cause: A hole, possibly from an octopus (one photographed shell)
Cause not documented in our sources

remains.text: After the animal dies, the empty shell may be recycled by hermit crabs and other organisms as a portable home, a pattern well documented across gastropod shells in general.
Growth increments and marks on the shell surface are the basis researchers use to estimate a cone snail's age, underlying the genus-wide 10-20 year lifespan estimate.

collecting.text: Never handle a live cone snail: C. textile can sting via a hollow, harpoon-like radular tooth that injects venom, normally used to subdue molluscan prey.

Among roughly 700 Conus species, confirmed multi-fatality human stings are attributed only to a different species (C. geographus); older reports of human deaths from C. textile specifically have not been adequately verified in the peer-reviewed literature.

pattern.description: A thick, heavy, off-white shell with four to six deep radial folds ending in big triangular points; between them shows a yellowish-brown to olive-green mantle dotted with brilliant blue-green rings.

egg.text: One spawning releases about 500 million eggs; a fertilised egg hatches into a swimming larva within 12 to 24 hours.

larva.text: The larva grows a shell, swims and feeds on tiny algae, then grows a foot and settles about 6 to 14 days after fertilisation.

maturity.text: Matures as a male at around 6 years and as a female by 9 to 10 years.

lifespan.text: Maximum lifespan is unknown; the oldest reliably aged true giant clam was 63 years old.

deaths.cause: Eaten by a fish biting its mantle
Shell crushed or drilled by a crab or snail while young
Harvested by people for meat and shell
Bleached by hot water and lost its algae
Cause not documented in our sources

remains.text: Shells of long-dead clams can lie buried in the reef; in the South China Sea boats have dug them out for carving, wrecking the reef.

collecting.text: Listed in CITES Appendix II, assessed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN and proposed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act. Do not take or buy giant clam shells.

remains.text: Hermit crabs move into empty snail shells and use them as portable homes.
A neat hole can mean a predator: moon snails, murex snails, octopuses, crabs and birds can all pierce shells.
On the shore, waves and sand roll and wear the shell; abrasion alone can even make holes.
